   104→
   105→## 📊 Labels Format
   106→
   107→Create `labels.csv` in your recordings directory:
   108→
   109→```csv
   110→filename,query_idx,text
   111→person1_schedule.wav,0,"Show me the schedule"
   112→person1_booth.wav,1,"Find a booth"
   113→person1_room.wav,2,"Navigate to room"
   114→person2_schedule.wav,0,"Display the schedule"
   115→person2_booth.wav,1,"Where is the booth"
   116→```
   117→
   118→**Columns:**
   119→- `filename`: Audio file name (in same directory)
   120→- `query_idx`: Query index (0-9 for 10 queries)
   121→- `text`: Exact text spoken (must match dataset variations)
   122→
   123→**Query indices** (from `audio_semantic_xtts.ipynb`):
   124→```
   125→0: Show me the schedule
   126→1: Find a booth
   127→2: Navigate to room
   128→3: Add a contact
   129→4: Take a note
   130→5: View the map
   131→6: Check messages
   132→7: See my profile
   133→8: Join a session
   134→9: Connect with someone
   135→```

   139→## 📈 Expected Results
   140→
   141→| Strategy | Effort | Improvement |
   142→|----------|--------|-------------|
   143→| **Baseline (XTTS only)** | - | 24.5% pair, 100% base |
   144→| **+ 50 real voices** | 2h | 60-70% accuracy |
   145→| **+ 100 real voices** | 3h | 70-80% accuracy |
   146→| **+ 200 real voices** | 4h | 80-90% accuracy |

   151→
   152→## 🛠️ Tools & Scripts
   153→
   154→### Check Audio Quality
   155→```python
   156→import librosa
   157→import numpy as np
   158→
   159→audio, sr = librosa.load('recording.wav')
   160→
   161→# RMS level (should be 0.1-0.5)
   162→rms = np.sqrt(np.mean(audio**2))
   163→print(f"RMS: {rms:.3f}")
   164→
   165→# Clipping (should be 0)
   166→clipped = np.sum(np.abs(audio) > 0.99)
   167→print(f"Clipped samples: {clipped}")
   168→
   169→# Duration
   170→duration = len(audio) / sr
   171→print(f"Duration: {duration:.2f} sec")
   172→```
   173→
   174→### Batch Convert Audio
   175→```bash
   176→# Convert all M4A to WAV
   177→for f in *.m4a; do
   178→    ffmpeg -i "$f" -ar 16000 -ac 1 "${f%.m4a}.wav"
   179→done
   180→
   181→# Normalize volume
   182→for f in *.wav; do
   183→    ffmpeg -i "$f" -filter:a "volume=1.5" -ar 16000 "norm_$f"
   184→done
   185→```
   186→
   187→### Generate Labels CSV
   188→```python
   189→import os
   190→import csv
   191→
   192→# Mapping of keywords to query indices
   193→query_map = {
   194→    'schedule': 0,
   195→    'booth': 1,
   196→    'room': 2,
   197→    'contact': 3,
   198→    'note': 4,
   199→    'map': 5,
   200→    'message': 6,
   201→    'profile': 7,
   202→    'session': 8,
   203→    'connect': 9
   204→}
   205→
   206→# Auto-generate labels from filenames
   207→recordings_dir = 'real_recordings/'
   208→labels = []
   209→
   210→for filename in os.listdir(recordings_dir):
   211→    if not filename.endswith('.wav'):
   212→        continue
   213→
   214→    # Extract query from filename (e.g., "alice_schedule.wav")
   215→    for keyword, idx in query_map.items():
   216→        if keyword in filename.lower():
   217→            labels.append({
   218→                'filename': filename,
   219→                'query_idx': idx,
   220→                'text': f'Automatically detected: {keyword}'
   221→            })
   222→            break
   223→
   224→# Save to CSV
   225→with open('labels.csv', 'w', newline='') as f:
   226→    writer = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=['filename', 'query_idx', 'text'])
   227→    writer.writeheader()
   228→    writer.writerows(labels)
   229→
   230→print(f"Generated labels for {len(labels)} recordings")
   231→```

   238→1. ✅ Record 5 people × 10 queries = 50 samples

   244→### Phase 2: Production Polish (1 Week)

   246→2. ✅ Add data augmentation (noise, reverb)
   247→3. ✅ Fine-tune 200 epochs
   248→4. ✅ Test accuracy → Expect 80-90%
   249→5. ✅ A/B test with users
   250→6. ✅ Iterate on failure cases
   251→
   252→### Phase 3: Continuous Improvement
   253→1. ✅ Deploy with feedback mechanism
   254→2. ✅ Collect user corrections weekly
   255→3. ✅ Fine-tune incrementally
   256→4. ✅ Gradual improvement to 95%+

   277→
   278→## ❓ FAQ
   279→
   280→### Q: How many recordings do I need?
   281→**A:** Minimum 50 (2-4 hours), recommended 200+ (1-2 days) for production.
   282→
   283→### Q: What if I don't have 10 people?
   284→**A:** 5 people is enough if they have diverse accents/ages. Quality > quantity.
   285→
   286→### Q: Can I add new queries?
   287→**A:** Yes! See "Strategy 4" in FINE_TUNING_GUIDE.md
   288→
   289→### Q: Will it forget XTTS training?
   290→**A:** Not if you use low learning rate (1e-4) and mix data 50:50.
   291→
   292→### Q: Can ESP32 learn on-device?
   293→**A:** Yes, theoretically! See "On-Device Learning" section in guide.
   294→
   295→### Q: What's the best recording app?
   296→**A:** iOS: Voice Memos, Android: Easy Voice Recorder, Desktop: Audacity
   297→
   298→---
   299→
   300→## 🐛 Troubleshooting
   301→
   302→**Problem:** Low accuracy after fine-tuning
   303→- ✅ Check audio quality (RMS, clipping)
   304→- ✅ Use lower learning rate (1e-5 instead of 1e-4)
   305→- ✅ Mix with XTTS data (--mix-with-xtts flag)
   306→
   307→**Problem:** Model forgot XTTS knowledge
   308→- ✅ Use very low learning rate (1e-5 or 1e-6)
   309→- ✅ Train fewer epochs (50 instead of 100)
   310→- ✅ Always mix real + XTTS data
   311→
   312→**Problem:** Audio files have errors
   313→- ✅ Convert to 16kHz mono: `ffmpeg -i input.wav -ar 16000 -ac 1 output.wav`
   314→- ✅ Check duration: Minimum 1 second, recommended 2-5 seconds
   315→- ✅ Normalize volume: Should not clip (max < 0.99)
   316→

     1→# 🧠 LLM Q&A Memorization PoC
     2→
     3→## Overview
     4→
     5→This is a **proof-of-concept notebook** that validates training a tiny instruction-tuned LLM for Q&A memorization that can run on ESP32-S3.
     6→
     7→## Quick Start (Google Colab)
     8→
     9→[![Open In Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/assets/colab-badge.svg)](https://colab.research.google.com/github/your-repo/badge/blob/main/workbench/tests/llm_qa_memorization_poc/qa_memorization_poc.ipynb)
    10→
    11→1. Upload `qa_memorization_poc.ipynb` to Google Colab
    12→2. Run all cells (Runtime → Run all)
    13→3. Wait ~15-30 minutes for training to complete
    14→4. Download the generated model files
    15→
    16→## What This PoC Does
    17→
    18→### Phase 1: Dataset Generation
    19→- Creates synthetic Q&A pairs from a sample profile
    20→- Generates ~50-100 Q&A pairs with 5x repetition
    21→- Formats data with special tokens: `<Q>question<A>answer</A>`
    22→
    23→### Phase 2: Custom Tokenizer
    24→- Trains a small BPE tokenizer (vocab=512) optimized for the Q&A domain
    25→- Includes special tokens for question/answer delimiters
    26→- Exports to llama2.c-compatible binary format
    27→
    28→### Phase 3: Model Training
    29→- **Quick PoC Config**: dim=128, layers=4, vocab=512 (~500K params)
    30→- Trains from scratch on Q&A pairs (pure memorization)
    31→- Massive overfitting (50-100 epochs) - this is the goal!
    32→- Training time: 10-20 minutes on Colab T4 GPU
    33→
    34→### Phase 4: Quantization
    35→- Exports to float32 format (~2MB)
    36→- Quantizes to int8 format (~500KB) - 4x compression!
    37→- Total package with tokenizer: <1MB
    38→
    39→### Phase 5: Inference Testing
    40→- Compiles llama2.c C inference code
    41→- Tests both float32 and int8 models
    42→- Validates memorization quality on test questions
    43→
    44→## Expected Results
    45→
    46→**Memory Footprint:**
    47→- Model (int8): ~500KB
    48→- Tokenizer: ~100-150KB
    49→- **Total: <1MB** (leaves 7MB for runtime in 8MB PSRAM!)
    50→
    51→**Quality:**
    52→- 80-90% success on exact/similar questions from training
    53→- Lower quality on heavily paraphrased questions (acceptable for PoC)
    54→
    55→**Performance:**
    56→- Training: 10-20 minutes
    57→- Inference: ~25-30 tok/s (estimated on ESP32-S3)
    58→
    59→## Scaling to Full Iteration
    60→
    61→Once PoC is validated, scale up:
    62→
    63→1. **Dataset**: 1000-2000 Q&A pairs generated from full profile using GPT-4/Claude
    64→2. **Model**: dim=224, layers=6, vocab=768 (~3.5M params → 3.5MB int8)
    65→3. **Training**:
    66→   - Phase 1: Pretrain on TinyStories (5-10K examples, 6-12 hours)
    67→   - Phase 2: Fine-tune on profile Q&A (1-2 hours)
    68→4. **Total memory**: ~4.1MB (model + tokenizer)
    69→
    70→## File Structure
    71→
    72→```
    73→llm_qa_memorization_poc/
    74→├── qa_memorization_poc.ipynb   # Main PoC notebook

    85→    ├── qa_output/

    89→    └── esp32_package/

    95→
    96→## Next Steps After PoC
    97→
    98→1. ✅ Validate concept works with tiny model
    99→2. Generate full dataset from complete profile using GPT-4
   100→3. Train larger model (3.5M params)

   103→
   104→## Notes
   105→
   106→- This PoC uses a **minimal config** for fast iteration (500K params)

     1→# microWakeWord Training Notebook
     2→
     3→Train custom wake word models compatible with ESP32-S3 using the microWakeWord framework.
     4→
     5→## Overview
     6→
     7→This notebook trains models that work with `wakeword_pretrained_test.ino`:
     8→- **Input**: 40-bin log-mel spectrogram (30ms window, 10ms stride)
     9→- **Architecture**: MixNet streaming model
    10→- **Output**: Quantized int8 TFLite model
    11→
    12→## Training Approach
    13→
    14→Based on [microWakeWord](https://github.com/kahrendt/microWakeWord):
    15→
    16→1. **Synthetic sample generation** - Piper TTS creates diverse voice samples
    17→2. **Data augmentation** - Background noise, reverb, pitch shift, EQ
    18→3. **Negative sampling** - Speech and noise datasets prevent false accepts
    19→4. **Streaming conversion** - Model runs frame-by-frame on ESP32
    20→
    21→## Quick Start
    22→
    23→1. Open `wakeword_training.ipynb` in Google Colab
    24→2. Wake word is pre-configured as "Hey Daisy" in Cell 4:
    25→   ```python
    26→   WAKE_WORD = "Hey Daisy"
    27→   PHONETIC_VARIATIONS = ["Hey Daisy", "hey daisy", "hey day zee", ...]
    28→   ```
    29→3. Run all cells (~30-60 minutes with GPU)
    30→4. Download `hey_daisy.tflite`
    31→5. Copy to SD card at `/models/`
    32→
    33→## Requirements
    34→
    35→- Google Colab with GPU runtime (recommended)
    36→- ~5GB disk space for datasets
    37→- Internet connection for downloads
    38→
    39→## Output Files
    40→
    41→- `{wake_word}.tflite` - Quantized model for ESP32
    42→- `{wake_word}.json` - Model manifest with parameters
    43→
    44→## Deployment
    45→
    46→1. Copy `.tflite` to SD card: `/models/hey_daisy.tflite`
    47→2. Update sketch:
    48→   ```cpp
    49→   #define MODEL_PATH "/models/hey_daisy.tflite"
    50→   ```
    51→3. Adjust detection parameters if needed:
    52→   ```cpp
    53→   #define PROBABILITY_CUTOFF  0.5f
    54→   #define SLIDING_WINDOW_SIZE 10
    55→   ```
    56→
    57→## Tuning Tips
    58→
    59→| Issue | Solution |
    60→|-------|----------|
    61→| Too many false positives | Increase `PROBABILITY_CUTOFF` |
    62→| Too many false negatives | Decrease `PROBABILITY_CUTOFF` |
    63→| Inconsistent detection | Add phonetic variations, retrain |
    64→| Model too large | Reduce architecture size |
    65→
    66→## Training Parameters
    67→
    68→Key settings in the notebook:
    69→
    70→| Parameter | Default | Description |
    71→|-----------|---------|-------------|
    72→| `SAMPLES_PER_COMBO` | 50 | Samples per voice/variation |
    73→| `training_steps` | 10000 | Total training iterations |
    74→| `negative_class_weight` | 20 | Penalty for false accepts |
    75→| `batch_size` | 128 | Training batch size |
    76→
    77→## Sources
    78→
    79→- [microWakeWord](https://github.com/kahrendt/microWakeWord) - Training framework
    80→- [micro-wake-word-models](https://github.com/esphome/micro-wake-word-models) - Pretrained models
    81→- [Piper TTS](https://github.com/rhasspy/piper) - Sample generation
    82→

     1→# YAMNet-1024 Audio Embedding on ESP32-S3
     2→
     3→Extract 1024-dimensional audio embeddings using YAMNet on ESP32-S3 with dual-core optimization.
     4→
     5→## Overview
     6→
     7→This sketch:
     8→1. **Records 3-5 seconds** of audio from dual INMP441 microphones (downmixed to mono)
     9→2. **Generates mel-spectrogram** (64 mels × 96 frames) using ESP-DSP accelerated FFT
    10→3. **Runs YAMNet-1024 inference** with TensorFlow Lite Micro (dual-core optimized)
    11→4. **Extracts 1024-D embeddings** from the model
    12→5. **Saves to SD card** as JSON format
    13→
    14→## Hardware Requirements
    15→
    16→- **ESP32-S3-LCD-2** board (or any ESP32-S3 with PSRAM)
    17→- **2× INMP441** MEMS microphones (I2S)
    18→- **SD card** (FAT32 formatted, 4GB+ recommended)
    19→- **Micro SD card reader/writer** (for loading model file)
    20→
    21→## Arduino IDE Setup
    22→
    23→### 1. Install Arduino Libraries
    24→
    25→Open Arduino IDE → Tools → Manage Libraries, then install:
    26→
    27→**Required:**
    28→- `TensorFlowLite_ESP32` by Kazuhiro Tanaka
    29→- (ESP-DSP is included with ESP32 Arduino core)
    30→
    31→**Note:** ESP-DSP library is built into the ESP32 Arduino core (esp-dsp component).
    32→
    33→### 2. Board Configuration
    34→
    35→- **Board:** ESP32S3 Dev Module
    36→- **Partition Scheme:** 16MB Flash (3MB APP/9MB FATFS)
    37→- **PSRAM:** OPI PSRAM
    38→- **Upload Speed:** 921600
    39→- **Core Debug Level:** None (or Info for debugging)
    40→
    41→## Model Download and Setup
    42→
    43→### Download YAMNet TFLite Model
    44→
    45→**Official Source: Kaggle (Recommended)**
    46→
    47→1. Visit: https://www.kaggle.com/models/google/yamnet/tfLite/classification-tflite/1
    48→2. Click "Download" button (requires free Kaggle account)
    49→3. Download: `yamnet_classification.tflite` (approx. 3.5-4 MB)
    50→
    51→**Alternative: Convert from TensorFlow Hub**
    52→```python
    53→# Python script to convert YAMNet to TFLite
    54→import tensorflow_hub as hub
    55→import tensorflow as tf
    56→
    57→model = hub.load('https://tfhub.dev/google/yamnet/1')
    58→# ... conversion code (see Kaggle yamnet-tflite notebook)
    59→```
    60→
    61→**For STMicroelectronics YAMNet-256 (smaller, faster)**
    62→- GitHub: https://github.com/STMicroelectronics/stm32ai-modelzoo
    63→- Navigate to: `audio_event_detection/yamnet/ST_pretrainedmodel_public_dataset/`
    64→- Choose ESC-10 or FSD50K dataset folder
    65→- Download: `yamnet_256_64x96_tl_int8.tflite` (~167 KB)
    66→
    67→### Prepare SD Card
    68→
    69→1. Format SD card as **FAT32**
    70→2. Rename the downloaded model file to: `yamnet.tflite`
    71→   - From Kaggle: `yamnet_classification.tflite` → `yamnet.tflite`
    72→   - From STM32: `yamnet_256_64x96_tl_int8.tflite` → `yamnet.tflite`
    73→3. Copy `yamnet.tflite` to the **root directory** of SD card
    74→4. Insert SD card into ESP32-S3-LCD-2
    75→
    76→The SD card structure should look like:
    77→```
    78→SD:/
    79→├── yamnet.tflite        (model file, 167KB-4MB depending on version)
    80→└── embedding.json       (will be created by sketch)
    81→```
    82→
    83→## Wiring Diagram
    84→
    85→### INMP441 Microphones → ESP32-S3 (I2S0)
    86→
    87→```
    88→ESP32-S3-LCD-2          INMP441 #1 (LEFT)      INMP441 #2 (RIGHT)
    89→────────────────        ─────────────────      ──────────────────
    90→3.3V ───────────┬────── VDD                    VDD
    91→                │
    92→GND ────────────┼────── GND ──────────┬─────── GND
    93→                │                     │
    94→GPIO 2 (BCK) ───┼────── SCK ──────────┼─────── SCK
    95→GPIO 4 (WS) ────┼────── WS ───────────┼─────── WS
    96→GPIO 18 (DIN) ──┴────── SD ───────────┴─────── SD
    97→                        │                      │
    98→                        L/R → GND              L/R → 3.3V
    99→                          (LEFT)                 (RIGHT)
   100→```
   101→
   102→**Pin Summary:**
   103→| Function      | ESP32 Pin | Device Pin     |
   104→|---------------|-----------|----------------|
   105→| Bit Clock     | GPIO 2    | SCK (both mics)|
   106→| Word Select   | GPIO 4    | WS (both mics) |
   107→| Data In       | GPIO 18   | SD (both mics) |
   108→| Left Channel  | —         | Mic #1 L/R → GND |
   109→| Right Channel | —         | Mic #2 L/R → 3.3V |
   110→
   111→### SD Card (SPI)
   112→
   113→SD card uses the built-in SD slot on ESP32-S3-LCD-2:
   114→- **CS:** GPIO 41
   115→- **MOSI:** GPIO 38
   116→- **MISO:** GPIO 40
   117→- **SCK:** GPIO 39
   118→
   119→## Upload and Run
   120→
   121→1. Connect ESP32-S3-LCD-2 to computer via USB-C
   122→2. Open `yamnet_audio_embedding.ino` in Arduino IDE
   123→3. Select board and port
   124→4. Click **Upload**
   125→5. Open **Serial Monitor** at **115200 baud**
   126→
   127→## Expected Output
   128→

   198→
   199→## Configuration
   200→
   201→Edit these constants in `yamnet_audio_embedding.ino`:
   202→
   203→```cpp
   204→const int RECORD_SECONDS = 3;  // Change to 3, 4, or 5 seconds
   205→```
   206→
   207→## Output Format
   208→
   209→The sketch creates `/embedding.json` on the SD card:
   210→
   211→```json
   212→{
   213→  "dimension": 1024,
   214→  "embeddings": [
   215→    0.234567,
   216→    -0.123456,
   217→    0.567890,
   218→    ...
   219→    (1024 values total)
   220→  ]
   221→}
   222→```
   223→
   224→## Memory Usage
   225→
   226→**PSRAM Allocation:**
   227→- Audio buffer (3 sec @ 16kHz): ~96 KB
   228→- Mel-spectrogram (64×96): ~24 KB
   229→- Model weights: ~3.9 MB
   230→- Tensor arena: 400 KB
   231→- Embeddings: 4 KB
   232→- **Total: ~4.4 MB** (fits comfortably in 8 MB PSRAM)
   233→
   234→**Heap Usage:**
   235→- TFLite infrastructure: ~50 KB
   236→- ESP-DSP FFT buffers: ~10 KB
   237→
   238→## Performance
   239→
   240→**Typical timing on ESP32-S3 @ 240MHz:**
   241→- Recording (3 sec): ~3000 ms
   242→- Mel-spectrogram: ~500 ms
   243→- YAMNet-1024 inference: **6-10 seconds** (dual-core optimized)
   244→- JSON write: ~150 ms
   245→- **Total: ~10-14 seconds**
   246→
   247→The inference is the bottleneck. YAMNet-1024 has 3.2M parameters - impressive for a microcontroller!
   248→
   249→## Troubleshooting
   250→
   251→### "Failed to load model from SD"
   252→- Check SD card is inserted
   253→- Verify `yamnet1024.tflite` exists in root directory
   254→- Try reformatting SD card as FAT32
   255→- Check file size is ~3-4 MB
   256→
   257→### "AllocateTensors() failed"
   258→- Model is too large or incompatible
   259→- Try increasing `TENSOR_ARENA_SIZE` in `yamnet_inference.h`
   260→- Check PSRAM is enabled in Arduino IDE settings
   261→
   262→### "Invoke() failed"
   263→- Model operations not supported
   264→- Check Serial Monitor for TFLite error messages
   265→- May need to add more ops to resolver in `yamnet_inference.cpp`
   266→
   267→### Very slow inference (>20 seconds)
   268→- Check CPU frequency is 240MHz (Tools → CPU Frequency)
   269→- Verify PSRAM is enabled
   270→- Model may be using PSRAM instead of SRAM (expected for large models)
   271→
   272→### Recording is silent
   273→- Check INMP441 wiring (GPIO 2, 4, 18)
   274→- Verify L/R pins: Mic #1 → GND, Mic #2 → 3.3V
   275→- Test with speaker_beep_test or dual_mic_sd_record
   276→
   277→### "Input tensor shape mismatch"
   278→- YAMNet expects [1, 96, 64, 1] or [1, 64, 96, 1]
   279→- Check model variant and adjust mel-spectrogram transpose if needed
   280→
   281→## Using a Smaller Model
   282→
   283→If YAMNet-1024 is too slow, use **YAMNet-256** instead:
   284→
   285→1. Download YAMNet-256 from STMicroelectronics:
   286→   ```
   287→   https://huggingface.co/STMicroelectronics/yamnet
   288→   ```
   289→
   290→2. Save as `yamnet256.tflite` on SD card
   291→
   292→3. Edit `yamnet_audio_embedding.ino`:
   293→   ```cpp
   294→   const char* MODEL_PATH = "/yamnet256.tflite";
   295→   ```
   296→
   297→4. Edit `yamnet_inference.h`:
   298→   ```cpp
   299→   #define EMBEDDING_DIM 256    // Change from 1024 to 256
   300→   ```
   301→
   302→YAMNet-256 is ~167 KB (fits in SRAM) and runs much faster (~1-2 seconds inference).
   303→
   304→## Technical Details
   305→
   306→### Mel-Spectrogram Preprocessing
   307→
   308→- **FFT size:** 512 (25ms window @ 16kHz)
   309→- **Hop length:** 160 samples (10ms)
   310→- **Mel bins:** 64
   311→- **Frames:** 96
   312→- **Frequency range:** 125-7500 Hz
   313→- **Window:** Hann window
   314→- **Transform:** Log mel-filterbank energies
   315→
   316→Preprocessing uses ESP-DSP's hardware-accelerated FFT for fast computation.
   317→
   318→### Dual-Core Optimization
   319→
   320→- **Core 0:** Main sketch, audio recording, mel-spectrogram
   321→- **Core 1:** TensorFlow Lite inference task
   322→
   323→This parallelization allows preprocessing to run concurrently with inference (though inference is still the bottleneck).
   324→
   325→### Model Architecture
   326→
   327→YAMNet-1024 uses MobileNetV1 architecture with depthwise-separable convolutions. The embedding layer (1024-D) sits before the final classification layer, capturing rich audio features.
   328→
   329→## Next Steps
   330→
   331→Once you have embeddings:
   332→
   333→1. **Audio similarity:** Compute cosine similarity between embeddings
   334→2. **Clustering:** Use k-means to group similar audio samples
   335→3. **Classification:** Train a simple classifier on top of embeddings
   336→4. **Voice identification:** Compare voice embeddings for speaker recognition
   337→5. **Anomaly detection:** Detect unusual sounds by embedding distance
   338→
   339→## References
   340→
   341→- [YAMNet Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.07850)
   342→- [TensorFlow Lite Micro](https://www.tensorflow.org/lite/microcontrollers)
   343→- [ESP-DSP Library](https://docs.espressif.com/projects/esp-dsp/)
   344→- [STMicroelectronics YAMNet](https://huggingface.co/STMicroelectronics/yamnet)
   345→

     1→# Fine-Tuning Guide for Audio-Text Semantic Model
     2→
     3→**Model:** XTTS-v2 + YAMNet + Contrastive Learning
     4→**Current Performance:** 24.5% pair accuracy, 100% base query accuracy
     5→**Target:** 80-95% with fine-tuning
     6→
     7→---
     8→
     9→## Table of Contents
    10→
    11→1. [Overview](#overview)
    12→2. [Fine-Tuning Strategies](#fine-tuning-strategies)
    13→3. [Code Examples](#code-examples)
    14→4. [Expected Improvements](#expected-improvements)
    15→5. [Production Workflows](#production-workflows)
    16→6. [Advanced Techniques](#advanced-techniques)
    17→7. [On-Device Learning](#on-device-learning)
    18→8. [Troubleshooting](#troubleshooting)
    19→
    20→---
    21→
    22→## Overview
    23→
    24→### Why Fine-Tune?
    25→
    26→The current model (trained on XTTS-v2 synthetic audio) achieves:
    27→- ✅ 100% base query matching (real use case)
    28→- ⚠️ 24.5% exact pair matching (strict metric)
    29→
    30→Fine-tuning with **real voice recordings** can improve this to **80-95%** accuracy.
    31→
    32→### What Can Be Fine-Tuned?
    33→
    34→1. **Audio projection head** (recommended) - Fast, effective
    35→2. **Text projection head** (optional) - If adding new query types
    36→3. **Both projections** (advanced) - Maximum flexibility
    37→4. **Training hyperparameters** - Squeeze more performance
    38→
    39→---
    40→
    41→## Fine-Tuning Strategies
    42→
    43→### Strategy 1: Add Real Voice Recordings ⭐ RECOMMENDED
    44→
    45→**Impact:** +60-70% accuracy improvement
    46→**Effort:** Medium
    47→**Timeline:** 2-4 hours
    48→
    49→**What you need:**
    50→- 5-10 people (diverse ages, genders, accents)
    51→- Each person records 1-2 variations per query
    52→- Total: 50-200 new audio samples
    53→
    54→**Benefits:**
    55→- YAMNet trained on real speech → better embeddings
    56→- Model learns actual voice patterns
    57→- Handles natural variations (pauses, emphasis, speed)
    58→
    59→**Process:**
    60→```bash
    61→# 1. Record audio (phone, laptop mic)
    62→# Save as WAV, 16kHz, mono
    63→
    64→# 2. Organize recordings
    65→real_recordings/
    66→├── person1_schedule.wav
    67→├── person1_booth.wav
    68→├── person2_schedule.wav
    69→└── ...
    70→
    71→# 3. Fine-tune model (see code below)
    72→```
    73→
    74→---
    75→
    76→### Strategy 2: Continue Training (More Epochs)
    77→
    78→**Impact:** +2-5% accuracy
    79→**Effort:** Very Low
    80→**Timeline:** 30-60 minutes
    81→
    82→**When to use:**
    83→- Model hasn't fully converged yet
    84→- Loss still decreasing at epoch 500
    85→- Quick performance boost
    86→
    87→**Process:**
    88→```python
    89→# Load existing model
    90→audio_projection = tf.keras.models.load_model('models_xtts/audio_projection.h5')
    91→
    92→# Continue training
    93→model = AudioTextModel(audio_projection, text_projection)
    94→model.compile(optimizer=tf.keras.optimizers.Adam(3e-4))

Based on my analysis of the Jupyter notebooks in `/home/alphons/project/OAISYS25/badge/workbench/tests/`, here are the key insights about the audio ML training methodologies:

## Audio Data Preparation

The notebooks use a **sophisticated multi-stage audio pipeline**:

1. **Raw Audio Generation**
   - Dual TTS engines: **Piper** (fast, ~100 samples/variation) and **XTTS-v2** (high-quality, 8 diverse speakers)
   - TED speaker samples (8 distinct voices: Bill Gates, Daphne Koller, etc.) for diversity
   - 2000+ Piper samples + 1600 XTTS samples = 3600+ training examples per concept
   - Confusable negatives: Partial phrases and similar-sounding words (3150 samples) to teach rejection

2. **Spectrogram Extraction**
   - **Mel-spectrograms**: 64 bins × 96 frames (optimized for ESP32)
   - Normalized to [0, 1], padded/trimmed to exact dimensions
   - Sample rate: 16kHz (standard for embedded audio)

3. **Audio Augmentation (Aggressive)**
   - AddGaussianNoise (0.5-2% amplitude)
   - TimeStretch (0.9-1.1x rate)
   - PitchShift (-2 to +2 semitones)
   - 2x multiplier per sample (original + augmented)

## Encoder Architectures Experimented With

The notebooks compare **three distinct approaches**:

### A. YAMNet + Projection (Large, Accurate)
- **YAMNet** (TensorFlow Hub): 1024-dim embeddings pre-trained on AudioSet
- Projection: 1024 → 256-dim via MLP (2 dense + BatchNorm + dropout)
- **Advantage**: Pre-trained on 521 sound classes, excellent semantic quality
- **Disadvantage**: Too large for ESP32 inference (requires TFLite)
- Dataset: 31,504 samples across 2008 unique questions
- **Accuracy**: Bucket matching ~50-70% (semantic similarity, not exact)

### B. Custom Audio Encoder (Small, Minimal)
- **Architecture**: Mini CNN on mel-spectrograms
  - Conv2D: 32→64→128→128 filters with MaxPooling
  - Global Average Pooling → Dense(256)
  - L2 normalization
- **Size**: ~273KB TFLite (int8 quantized)
- **Training**: 3360 samples (2 per question, male/female voice diversity)
- **Accuracy**: **100% top-1, 100% top-5** on training set (perfect memorization)
- **Key insight**: Direct mel→embedding without intermediate feature extraction works well on small datasets

### C. Fast Encoder (30-min training, 2 samples/question)
- Reduces dataset to 3360 samples (10% of full)
- Same CNN architecture as B
- **Training time**: ~2 hours total (vs. days for YAMNet approach)
- **Result**: Still achieves excellent accuracy with minimal data

## Training Objectives & Loss Functions

**Contrastive Learning** is the core methodology:

```
Loss = (loss_a2t + loss_t2a) / 2

where:
- logits = audio_emb @ text_emb^T / temperature
- loss_a2t = CrossEntropyLoss(labels, logits)  # audio to text
- loss_t2a = CrossEntropyLoss(labels, logits^T)  # text to audio
- temperature = 0.2 (controls contrast sharpness)
```

**Bucketed Sampling Strategy** (crucial insight):
- Groups similar questions into buckets (similarity threshold: 0.85)
- Each batch selects ONE audio per bucket
- Ensures negatives are truly different questions (not just audio variants)
- Result: Prevents contamination from similar paraphrases

## Model Quantization for ESP32

**Multi-stage Quantization Pipeline**:

1. **Float32 → Int8 Post-Training Quantization**
   ```
   - Representative dataset: 50-100 samples
   - Target ops: TFLITE_BUILTINS_INT8
   - Quantization error: <0.002 per layer (excellent)
   ```

2. **Size Reduction**
   - Float32: ~21-22 MB → Int8: ~6-7 MB (3-4x compression)
   - Audio encoder only: 273KB (tiny enough for inference + model in SRAM)

3. **Distillation Experiments**
   - YAMNet (1024-dim) → Custom encoder (256-dim)
   - Knowledge transfer via contrastive alignment
   - Minimal performance loss, huge size reduction

## End-to-End Training Attempts

### Single-Stage: Direct Audio→Intent (NOT Done)
- All notebooks use **multi-stage pipelines** instead
- Reason: Audio is high-dimensional; projecting to lower dims is standard practice

### Multi-Stage Pipeline (Actually Used)
1. **Phase 1**: Wake word detection (microWakeWord, streaming MixNet)
2. **Phase 2**: Audio embedding (YAMNet or custom CNN)
3. **Phase 3**: Similarity search (cosine distance to 2008 intent embeddings)
4. **Phase 4**: LLM response generation (llama2.c, 6M params)

**This is NOT end-to-end**, but each phase is independently optimizable and deployable.

## Multimodal Approaches Observed

While primarily **audio-centric**, the notebooks show **latent multimodality**:

### Audio-Text Alignment
- YAMNet embeddings (audio) aligned to MPNet/MiniLM embeddings (text)
- Both projected to shared 256-dim space
- Enables semantic search across modalities

### Wake Word + Q&A Fusion
- Wake word: Audio-only classification (does "Hey Daisy" match?)
- Q&A: Audio embedding → similarity search → text retrieval
- Response: Text generation via LLM

### Profile + Q&A Training
- **Text-to-audio**: GPT-generated prose + Q&A pairs
- **Audio-to-embedding**: YAMNet/CNN extracts from TTS-generated speech
- **Embedding-to-text**: Pre-computed 256-dim vectors stored as binary

## Key Design Patterns

1. **Bucketed Contrastive Learning**: Prevents question-level contamination
2. **Multi-GPU Data Generation**: 12 Vast.ai GPUs, parallel XTTS synthesis
3. **Streaming Feature Extraction**: ~0.96s frames per YAMNet output
4. **Binary Embedding Storage**: Float32 serialized as packed struct
5. **Custom Tokenizers**: SentencePiece BPE (1024 vocab) for LLM
6. **Resume Capability**: JSON state files for checkpointing (used extensively)

## Recommendations for ESP32

**Optimal Stack**:
- **Wake word**: microWakeWord (40-bin mel spectrogram, streaming MixNet)
- **Audio embedding**: Custom CNN (~300KB), trained on 2-4 samples/question
- **Similarity search**: Pre-computed 256-dim text embeddings in binary format
- **LLM**: llama2.c 1-3M quantized (~5-8MB), with 2000 Q&A memorization
- **Total**: ~15-20MB SD card footprint

The training approach is **pragmatic for embedded**: use pre-trained models where available (YAMNet), distill to smaller custom encoders, and rely on heavy memorization rather than generalization for constrained domains.

Excellent! I now have a comprehensive understanding of the pipeline. Let me create a detailed summary document:

## Comprehensive Voice-to-Text ML Pipeline Analysis

Based on my thorough exploration of the OAISYS Badge firmware, here is the complete architecture of the voice-to-text pipeline:

---

## COMPLETE DATA FLOW: Voice Input → Text Output

### Overall State Machine
```
LOGO_LOOP → (wake word) → RECORDING → EMBEDDING → SIMILARITY → LLM_INFERENCE → TTS_OUTPUT → LOGO_LOOP
              (detection)  (3-5 sec)   (process)   (search DB)   (generate text) (speak)
```

---

## PHASE 1: WAKE WORD DETECTION ("Hey Daisy")

### Audio Capture → Features → Detection

**Input Hardware:**
- Dual INMP441 microphones via I2S0 (BCK=GPIO2, WS=GPIO4, DIN=GPIO18)
- Sampling rate: 16 kHz, 16-bit samples

**Feature Extraction (MicStream):**
- Uses **Google microfrontend** library (speech recognition preprocessing)
- Output: **3 frames × 40 mel-spectrogram bins** = 120 uint16_t values per detection window
- Window parameters:
  - 30ms window size
  - 10ms stride (overlapping frames)
  - 40 mel-frequency bins
  - Samples every 10ms, provides new detection every ~30ms

**Model: wake_word.tflite**
- **Size:** 130 KB
- **Architecture:** microWakeWord-based CNN (EdgeNeuron TFLite compatible)
- **Input:** [1, 3, 40, 1] = (batch, frames, bins, channels) uint16_t or int8_t
- **Output:** Single scalar probability (0-1)
- **Memory:** 502KB tensor arena + 52KB variable arena = 554KB total

**Detection Logic (Sliding Window):**
```
Config (from wake_word.json):
  - probability_cutoff: 0.5 (average score threshold)
  - sliding_window_size: 10 frames
  - min_high_frames: 6 (frames above 0.5)
  - cooldown_ms: 1500 (prevent rapid re-triggers)

Trigger when:
  - Average probability >= 0.5
  - AND 6+ of 10 frames exceed 0.5
  - AND cooldown elapsed
```

**Output:** Boolean wake word detected

---

## PHASE 2: AUDIO RECORDING

**Recording Module (AudioRecorder):**
- **Duration:** 3-5 seconds (configured, default 3s)
- **Buffer:** PSRAM-allocated int16_t array
- **Capture:** 16 kHz × 3s = 48,000 samples = ~96 KB
- **Format:** Raw 16-bit mono PCM
- **Pre-processing:** Discards first 2 seconds of audio (mic stabilization), records last 1-3 seconds

**Output:** int16_t[48000] audio buffer in PSRAM

---

## PHASE 3: AUDIO EMBEDDING EXTRACTION

### Convert Speech → 256-Dimensional Vector

**Step 3a: Mel-Spectrogram Generation**

Uses ESP32-S3 hardware FFT acceleration (ESP-DSP library):

```
Input: int16_t[48000] @ 16kHz (3 seconds)
      ↓
Windowing (Hann window) + FFT:
  - FFT size: 512 samples (32ms @ 16kHz)
  - Hop length: 160 samples (10ms stride)
  - Number of frames: (48000 - 512) / 160 + 1 ≈ 297 frames → padded to 96 frames
  - Output: 257 frequency bins (FFT_SIZE/2 + 1)
      ↓
Mel-filterbank (125 Hz - 7.5 kHz):
  - 64 triangular mel filters
  - Replaces linear Hz with perceptually-motivated mel scale
      ↓
Log magnitude + Min-max normalization:
  - Log10 of power spectrum
  - Normalize to [0, 1] range per spectrogram
      ↓
Output: float[64 × 96] = 6,144 values
        (64 mel bins × 96 time frames)
```

**Computation Details:**
- SIMD-accelerated via `dsps_dotprod_f32_aes3` (ESP-DSP PIE SIMD)
- Approximately 50% of embedding time (~5-7 sec total)
- Allocations:
  - Mel filterbank: 64 × 257 × 4 bytes = 66 KB (16-byte aligned PSRAM)
  - Working buffers: ~2.5 MB PSRAM
  - Freed after inference

**Step 3b: CNN Embedding Model Inference**

**Model: audio_encoder.tflite**
- **Size:** 289 KB
- **Architecture:** Small CNN trained with contrastive learning to align audio with text
```
Input: [1, 64, 96, 1] float mel-spectrogram
  ↓
Conv2D(32) + ReLU → MaxPool2D(2,2) → [1, 32, 48, 32]
  ↓
Conv2D(64) + ReLU → MaxPool2D(2,2) → [1, 64, 24, 64]
  ↓
Conv2D(128) + ReLU → MaxPool2D(2,2) → [1, 128, 12, 128]
  ↓
Conv2D(128) + ReLU → GlobalAvgPool2D → [1, 128]
  ↓
Dense(256) → [1, 256]
  ↓
L2Normalization → Output: float[256]
```
- **Output:** 256-dimensional L2-normalized embedding vector
- **Memory:** 300 KB tensor arena
- **Inference time:** ~1-2 seconds

**Key Property:** L2-normalized means ||embedding||₂ = 1.0, enabling **cosine similarity** search.

**Output:** float[256] normalized embedding

---

## PHASE 4: EMBEDDING SIMILARITY SEARCH

### Match Audio Against Intent Database

**Search Database (Precomputed):**

**embeddings.bin** (2.0 MB):
- 2,008 × 256-dimensional float32 embeddings
- Each embedding trained to match one intent
- Total size: 2008 × 256 × 4 bytes = 2,064,384 bytes ≈ 2.0 MB
- Stored in PSRAM with 16-byte alignment for SIMD

**intents.txt** (63 KB):
- 2,008 lines, one intent per line
- Examples:
  ```
  What is Alphons email address
  What is his phone number
  When was Alphons born
  ...
  ```
- Stored in PSRAM, line offsets precomputed for O(1) lookup

**Search Algorithm: Linear Scan with Top-K Tracking**

```cpp
For each of 2,008 embeddings:
  1. Compute cosine similarity:
     score = (query · db_embedding) / (||query|| × ||db_embedding||)
     
     // Both are L2-normalized, so ||query|| = ||db_embedding|| = 1.0
     // Therefore: score = query · db_embedding
     
     // Implemented with SIMD: dsps_dotprod_f32_aes3()
     //   5-10x faster than scalar dot product
  
  2. Track top 5 matches for debugging
  
Output: Best match with score (0-1)
```

**Threshold Decision:**
```
score >= 0.3 (config: DEFAULT_EMBED_THRESHOLD)
  → Proceed to LLM inference
  
score < 0.3
  → Apologize: "Sorry, I could not understand that."
  → Return to logo loop (stash for later, Phase 8)
```

**Output:** SearchResult { intent_index, similarity_score (0-1), intent_text }

---

## PHASE 5: LLM INFERENCE (Text Generation)

### Generate Response from Intent

**LLM Model: llm_model.bin**
- **Size:** 6.0 MB
- **Architecture:** Quantized Llama2-style transformer
  - Q8_0 quantization (int8 weights + float32 per-group scales)
  - Adaptive to multiple model sizes (1M-6M parameters)
  - Default: ~260K-1M parameter TinyStories model
- **Model Parameters (from header):**
  - Dimension: 64-224 (model hidden size)
  - Hidden dim: 512-896 (FFN intermediate)
  - Layers: 4-8 transformer blocks
  - Attention heads: 8
  - KV heads: 4 (grouped query attention)
  - Vocabulary size: 512-1024
  - Max sequence length: 256 tokens
  - Group size (quantization): 32-64

**Tokenizer: tokenizer.bin (13 KB)**
- **Type:** BPE (Byte Pair Encoding), SentencePiece format
- **Vocab:** 512-1024 tokens
- **Encoding:** Converts text → token IDs
- **Decoding:** Converts token IDs → text pieces
- **Example:**
  ```
  "What is Alphons email" 
  → [tokenize] → [What][is][Alph][ons][email] 
  → [143, 73, 856, 299, 567]
  ```

**Inference Process: Token-by-Token Autoregressive Generation**

```
Input: User intent (e.g., "What is Alphons email address")
      ↓
[Prompt wrapping - adds special tokens]
      ↓
Encode prompt → token IDs
      ↓
LOOP until max_tokens or end token:
  1. Forward pass:
     - Input: previous token ID
     - Position: current position in sequence (for RoPE)
     - KV cache: stores previous keys/values for fast inference
     - Output: logits (vocab_size probabilities)
  
  2. Sample token:
     - Temperature: 0.8 (for some randomness vs. greedy)
     - Top-P: 0.9 (nucleus sampling - only top 90% cumulative prob)
     - Output: next token ID
  
  3. Decode token → text piece
     - Callback: `onLLMToken()` - stream to display in real-time
     - Accumulate in response string
  
  4. Update KV cache
      ↓
Output: Generated response string
```

**Quantization Impact:**
```
Int8 weights (16x smaller) + Per-group dequantization
  → Inference: ~80% speed of FP32
  → Accuracy: ~95% of FP32 (negligible difference for text generation)
  
Bottleneck: Memory bandwidth (PSRAM), not compute
  Most inference time spent loading weights from PSRAM
```

**Generation Config (from sd_data/config.json):**
```json
{
  "llm_temperature": 0.8,      // Higher = more randomness
  "llm_topp": 0.9,             // Keep top 90% cumulative prob
  "llm_max_tokens": 128        // Max response length
}
```

**Output:** String response (e.g., "Alphons' email address is alphons@example.com")

---

## PHASE 5b: TEXT-TO-SPEECH (RobotTTS)

**TTS Module: robot_tts.cpp** (via ESP32-SAM library)
- **Algorithm:** SAM (Software Automatic Mouth) - phoneme-based synthesis
- **Voice:** Robotic male (deterministic, small code footprint)
- **Input:** Response string
- **Output:** Audio via MAX98357A speaker (I2S1)

---

## MEMORY MANAGEMENT

### PSRAM Layout (8 MB available)

```
PSRAM Organization:
├─ Video buffer:        1.2 MB   (logo.mjpeg frame buffers)
├─ Audio encoder:       0.3 MB   (tensor arena)
├─ Wake word:           0.55 MB  (tensor arena + var arena)
├─ ML pool:             1.0 MB   (allocated but unuse by LLM)
├─ Recording buffer:    0.1 MB   (3 sec @ 16kHz × 2 bytes)
├─ Embeddings:          2.0 MB   (2008 × 256-dim float32)
├─ Intents:             0.1 MB   (63 KB text)
├─ LLM model (when active): 6.0 MB
└─ Working buffers:     Variable

Critical Constraint:
  Video (1.2) + Embeddings (2.0) + LLM (6.0) > 8 MB total
  
Solution: Model swapping!
  1. Keep embeddings and video resident (3.2 MB)
  2. Before LLM: Free video (unloadVideo()) + embeddings (end())
  3. Load LLM (6.0 MB) - fits in freed space
  4. After LLM: Reload video + embeddings
```

### Model Loading/Unloading

```cpp
STATE_LOGO_LOOP:
  - Wake word loaded (uses mlPool)
  - Video resident (1.2 MB)
  - Embeddings resident (2.0 MB)

STATE_EMBEDDING:
  - Load audio encoder (uses mlPool)
  - Total: 0.3 MB (reuses 1MB mlPool)

STATE_SIMILARITY:
  - Unload audio encoder
  - Embeddings ready for search

STATE_LLM_INFERENCE:
  - Free: Video (1.2), Embeddings (2.0), mlPool (1.0) = 4.2 MB freed
  - Load: LLM (6.0 MB) - fits!
  - Inference happens

STATE_TTS_OUTPUT / back to LOGO_LOOP:
  - Unload: LLM (6.0)
  - Reload: Video (1.2 MB), Embeddings (2.0 MB), mlPool (1.0 MB)
```

## KEY METRICS & PERFORMANCE

### Model Sizes (SD Card)
```
wake_word.tflite      130 KB
audio_encoder.tflite  289 KB
llm_model.bin         6.0 MB
tokenizer.bin         13 KB
embeddings.bin        2.0 MB
intents.txt           63 KB
Total:               ~8.5 MB (all models + data resident on SD)
```

### Input/Output Dimensions

| Stage | Input | Output | Size |
|-------|-------|--------|------|
| Audio Capture | 16kHz raw | 40×3 features | 120 uint16 |
| Mel-Spectrogram | int16[48000] | float[64×96] | 6,144 float |
| Audio Encoder | float[64×96] | float[256] | 256 float |
| Similarity Search | float[256] | intent + score | string + float |
| LLM Input | tokens (32-bit IDs) | — | max 256 tokens |
| LLM Output | logits[vocab_size] | token ID | 1 int32 |
| TTS Input | text string | audio samples | variable |

### Processing Times (Estimated)

```
Wake word detection:     ~30ms per frame (real-time, continuous)
Recording:              3-5 seconds (user duration)
Mel-spectrogram:        5-7 seconds total embedding time
Audio encoder:          1-2 seconds (CNN inference)
Embedding search:       100-200ms (linear scan × 2008)
LLM generation:         10-20 seconds (token-by-token, temperature sampling)
TTS output:             variable (depends on response length)
```

### Audio Processing Chain

```
Raw audio (INMP441):
  16 kHz, stereo capable → mono @ 16 kHz
      ↓
Microfrontend (wake word):
  40-bin log-mel spectrogram
  30ms windows, 10ms stride
      ↓
I2S DMA capture → PSRAM audio buffer
      ↓
Recording (AudioRecorder):
  Raw 16-bit samples to buffer
      ↓
Embedding (AudioEmbedder):
  Mel-spectrogram generation + CNN → 256-dim vector
```

---

## WAKE WORD DETECTION SPECIFICS

**Microfrontend Features:**
- 40 mel-frequency bins (125 Hz - 8000 Hz range)
- 3 consecutive frames = 30ms of context
- Overlapping 10ms stride provides dense sampling
- Updated every ~30ms during listening

**Model (microWakeWord):**
- Binary classifier: target word vs. non-target
- Lightweight CNN optimized for on-device inference
- Probability output: 0.0 (negative) to 1.0 (positive)

**Detection Statistics (from config):**
```json
{
  "probability_cutoff": 0.5,           // Avg score threshold
  "sliding_window_average_size": 10,   // Frames to average
  "min_high_frames": 6,                // Min frames > 0.5
  "min_frame_prob": 0.5,               // Individual frame threshold
  "cooldown_ms": 1500                  // Debounce time
}
```

---

## EMBEDDING/SIMILARITY SPECIFICS

**Embedding Space Properties:**
- **Dimension:** 256
- **Normalization:** L2 (unit length vectors)
- **Similarity Metric:** Cosine similarity = dot product (since L2-normalized)
- **Score Range:** -1 to 1 (typically 0 to 1 for similar vectors)

**Database:**
- **Size:** 2,008 embeddings (one per intent)
- **Organization:** 
  - embeddings.bin: contiguous float32 array
  - intents.txt: corresponding intent text (newline-delimited)
  - Offset table: pre-computed indices for O(1) intent lookup

**Search Complexity:**
- Linear scan: O(n) where n=2008
- Per-embedding: One dot product + normalization
- SIMD acceleration: 5-10x speedup via ESP-DSP
- Total search time: ~100-200ms

**Threshold Strategy:**
```
Config: embed_threshold = 0.3

Rationale:
  - 0.3 = fairly confident match in 256-dim space
  - Above 0.3: proceed to LLM
  - Below 0.3: too uncertain, apologize

Tunable via config.json for better precision/recall tradeoff
```

---

## LLM ARCHITECTURE DETAILS

**Quantization Format (Q8_0):**
```
Per-group quantization:
  - Group size: 32-64 (read from model header)
  - Each group: [int8[32], float32 scale]
  - Dequantization: value = int8 * scale
  - Reduces weights: FP32 (4 bytes) → INT8 (1 byte) = 4x compression
  - Minimal accuracy loss (<5%)
```

**Transformer Blocks (repeated n_layers times):**
```
For each layer:
  1. RMSNorm(input) → normalized
  2. MultiHeadAttention:
     - Q = W_q @ normalized
     - K = W_k @ normalized
     - V = W_v @ normalized
     - Attention scores (RoPE positional encoding)
     - KV cache: stores K, V for fast re-inference
  3. Output projection: W_o @ attention_output
  4. RMSNorm again
  5. FFN (3 matrices: W1, W2, W3):
     - hidden = SiLU(W1 @ x) ⊙ W3 @ x  (gated)
     - output = W2 @ hidden
```

**KV Cache:**
```
Why needed:
  In autoregressive generation, each new token must attend to all previous tokens.
  Without cache: O(n²) computation for n-token sequence.
  With cache: O(n) - only compute one more attention row.

Storage:
  [n_layers, seq_len, n_kv_heads, head_size]
  For 256 max tokens: ~512 KB PSRAM
```

**Token Generation Loop:**
```cpp
for token_id in 1..max_tokens:
  logits = forward(model, token_id, position)
  next_token_id = sample(logits, temperature, top_p)
  text_piece = decode(tokenizer, next_token_id)
  callback(text_piece)  // Stream to display
  position++

Stops when:
  - EOS (end-of-sequence) token generated
  - max_tokens reached
  - Or manually stopped
```

---

## SYSTEM CONSTRAINTS & TRADEOFFS

### Memory Bottleneck
```
PSRAM: 8 MB total
  - Can't fit video + embeddings + LLM simultaneously
  - Solution: Model swapping (unload unused, load needed)
  - Swap overhead: ~2 seconds (SD I/O + allocation)
```

### Speed Bottleneck
```
LLM inference: 10-20 seconds for 128 tokens
  - Bottleneck: PSRAM memory bandwidth (not CPU)
  - Each forward pass requires reading ~6 MB of weights
  - ~100-200ms per token on ESP32-S3
```

### Wake Word Robustness
```
Challenges:
  - Mic noise variations
  - User voice variations
  - Ambient audio

Mitigation:
  - Sliding window averaging (vote over 10 frames)
  - Cooldown (prevent rapid false triggers)
  - Tunable thresholds (config.json)
```

### Embedding Collision Risk
```
With 2,008 intents and 256-dim embeddings:
  - Curse of dimensionality means similarity scores are biased toward 0.5
  - Need good embedding training (contrastive loss)
  - Threshold of 0.3 is conservative but safe
  - False positives rare; false negatives more likely at high threshold
```

## SUMMARY: COMPLETE PIPELINE

```
HARDWARE: INMP441 mic → I2S0 RX → ESP32-S3 @ 240MHz dual-core

USER: Says "Hey Daisy, what is my email?"
  │
  ├─ [PHASE 1: WAKE WORD]
  │  Raw audio → 40×3 features every 30ms
  │  TFLite model (130KB) → Probability
  │  Sliding window → Detection (0.5 threshold)
  │  
  ├─ [PHASE 2: RECORDING]
  │  Record 3 seconds → int16[48000] to PSRAM
  │  
  ├─ [PHASE 3: EMBEDDING]
  │  Mel-spectrogram (64×96) → ESP-DSP FFT (7s)
  │  CNN encoder (289KB) → float[256] L2-normalized (2s)
  │  
  ├─ [PHASE 4: SIMILARITY SEARCH]
  │  Linear scan 2008 embeddings
  │  Cosine similarity (SIMD dot products)
  │  Best match: "What is Alphons email address" (score 0.78)
  │  
  ├─ [PHASE 5: LLM INFERENCE]
  │  Q8_0 quantized transformer (6MB)
  │  Token-by-token generation with temperature sampling
  │  "Alphons' email address is alphons@example.com"
  │  Display streams in real-time
  │  
  └─ [PHASE 5b: TTS OUTPUT]
     SAM synthesizer → Speaker output
     Return to LOGO_LOOP

TOTAL LATENCY: ~20-30 seconds
  Wake word: <1s
  Recording: 3-5s
  Embedding: ~7s
  Search: <0.5s
  LLM: 10-20s
  TTS: 2-5s
```

cat > /tmp/ml_experiments_summary.txt << 'EOF'
COMPREHENSIVE ML TRAINING PIPELINES SUMMARY
OAISYS25 Badge Conference Device
================================================================================

PROJECT STRUCTURE
The badge firmware implements an AI assistant that can:
1. Record wake words and user queries
2. Embed audio queries semantically
3. Search embeddings for intent matching
4. Generate personalized responses via LLM
5. Convert text responses to speech

This requires 5 parallel ML pipelines, all deployed on ESP32-S3 (8MB PSRAM).

================================================================================
EXPERIMENT 1: AUDIO EMBEDDING DATASET TRAINING
Directory: audio_embedding_dataset_ipynb/
Purpose: Generate large-scale audio-text dataset for contrastive learning
================================================================================

APPROACH:
- Parallelized dataset generation across 12 GPUs
- Generate 32K audio samples with semantic annotations
- Create audio-text projection models for similarity search

ARCHITECTURE:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Audio-Text Embedding Model (Contrastive Learning)              │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                 │
│  Audio (16kHz) ──→ XTTS-v2 ──→ YAMNet ──→ 1024-D audio feat  │
│                                                                 │
│                                      ↓ Dense(512) + BN          │
│                              Audio Projection (1024→256)         │
│                                      ↓                           │
│                                  256-D embedded                  │
│                                      ↑                           │
│                    Contrastive Loss (Temperature=0.2)            │
│                                      ↑                           │
│                                  256-D embedded                  │
│                              Text Projection (384→256)           │
│                                      ↓ Dense                     │
│                                                                 │
│  Text Query ──→ MiniLM-L6-v2 ──────→ 384-D text feat          │
│                                                                 │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

MODELS & CONFIGURATIONS:

1. Audio Projection:
   - Input: 1024-D (YAMNet embeddings)
   - Layers: Dense(512) [ReLU] → BatchNorm → Dropout(0.2) → Dense(256) → L2-norm
   - Output: 256-D normalized embeddings
   - Size (Keras H5): 2.6 MB
   - Size (TFLite quantized): 664 KB

2. Text Projection:
   - Input: 384-D (MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings)
   - Layers: BatchNorm → Dense(256) → L2-norm
   - Output: 256-D normalized embeddings
   - Size (Keras H5): 2.1 MB
   - Size (TFLite): 527 KB

3. Audio Encoder (Optional acceleration):
   - Specialized TFLite model: 289 KB
   - Speeds up on-device encoding

TRAINING CONFIGURATION:
- Loss Function: Contrastive (NT-Xent) with temperature=0.2
- Optimizer: Adam @ 3e-4 learning rate
- Batch Aggregation: Bucketed sampling (12 GPUs)
- Data Augmentation: Gaussian noise on audio
- Epochs: 500 (from baseline gTTS model)

INPUT DATA:
- Queries: 10 conference badge questions
- Speakers: Diverse (generated via XTTS-v2 synthetic speech)
- Augmentations: 2× per sample (original + noise)
- Total samples generated: ~32K audio files

DATASET STRUCTURE:
  Per query bucket:
  ├── q0000_s0.wav        (speaker 0, original)
  ├── q0000_s0_aug.wav    (speaker 0, augmented)
  ├── q0000_s1.wav        (speaker 1, original)
  ├── q0000_s1_aug.wav    (speaker 1, augmented)
  └── ... (multiple speakers)

RESULTS:
- Pair matching accuracy: 24.5% (vs 4% with gTTS baseline)
- Base query matching: 100% (real use case metric)
- Output embeddings.bin: 2.0 MB (300 embeddings × 256-D float32)
- Output intents.txt: 63 KB (query text annotations)

KEY FILES GENERATED:
  models/
  ├── audio_projection.h5 (2.6 MB, trainable)
  ├── audio_projection_quantized.tflite (664 KB, deployable)
  ├── text_projection.h5 (2.1 MB, trainable)
  ├── text_projection.tflite (527 KB, deployable)
  ├── audio_encoder.tflite (289 KB, optional)
  ├── embeddings.bin (2.0 MB, pre-computed)
  └── intents.txt (63 KB)

DEPLOYMENT STRATEGY:
- Deploy TFLite versions to ESP32 (total ~1.5 MB)
- Pre-compute query embeddings on server
- On-device: Record audio → YAMNet embedding → Cosine similarity with query embeddings
- Inference on ESP32: ~100-200ms for similarity search

================================================================================
EXPERIMENT 2: AUDIO SEMANTIC XTTS FINE-TUNING
Directory: audio_semantic_xtts_ipynb/
Purpose: Fine-tune audio-text embeddings with human voice recordings
================================================================================

APPROACH:
- Generate synthetic baseline with XTTS-v2 (human-quality TTS)
- Fine-tune projection heads with real voice recordings
- Achieve 80-95% accuracy with domain-specific voices

BASELINE ARCHITECTURE (XTTS-v2 vs gTTS):
┌──────────────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────┐
│ gTTS (Google Text-to-Speech)         │ XTTS-v2 (Coqui TTS)               │
├──────────────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Pair accuracy: 4%                    │ Pair accuracy: 24.5%              │
│ Quality: Robotic                     │ Quality: Human-like               │
│ Voices: Limited                      │ Voices: Diverse, natural          │
│ Inference: Fast                      │ Inference: Slower (but still fast)│
│ YAMNet match: Poor (unnatural audio) │ YAMNet match: Excellent           │
└──────────────────────────────────────┴────────────────────────────────────┘

FINE-TUNING STRATEGIES (RECOMMENDED):

Strategy 1: Add Real Voice Recordings (RECOMMENDED)
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Improvement Curve: ~24.5% (baseline) → 60-90% (with real audio)│
│ Effort: 2-4 hours                                               │
│ Result: Better generalization to diverse speaker voices         │
│                                                                 │
│ Requirements:                                                   │
│   - 5-10 people (diverse ages, genders, accents)               │
│   - 1-2 variations per query per person                         │
│   - Total: 50-200 samples                                       │
│   - Format: WAV, 16kHz, mono                                    │
│                                                                 │
│ Process:                                                        │
│   1. Record audio (phone/laptop mic)                            │
│   2. Create labels.csv mapping                                  │
│   3. Run fine-tuning (100-200 epochs)                          │
│   4. Deploy to ESP32                                            │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

IMPLEMENTATION OPTIONS:

Option A: Notebook-based (Google Colab recommended):
  1. Load pre-trained model
  2. Prepare real voice dataset
  3. Fine-tune audio_projection head
  4. Export quantized TFLite
  5. Deploy to ESP32

Option B: Script-based (finetune_example.py):
  1. Prepare real recordings directory
  2. Generate labels.csv
  3. Run: python finetune_example.py --real-voices <dir> --epochs 100
  4. Convert to TFLite if needed
  5. Deploy

EXPECTED PERFORMANCE IMPROVEMENTS:

┌──────────────────────┬──────────┬──────────────────────────────┐
│ Scenario             │ Effort   │ Improvement                  │
├──────────────────────┼──────────┼──────────────────────────────┤
│ Continue training    │ <30 min  │ +2-5%                        │
│ Add 50 real voices   │ 2 hours  │ +35-45% → 60-70% total       │
│ Add 100 real voices  │ 3 hours  │ +45-55% → 70-80% total       │
│ Add 200+ real voices │ 4+ hours │ +55-65% → 80-95% total       │
└──────────────────────┴──────────┴──────────────────────────────┘

KEY FEATURES:
- Batch normalization stabilizes training
- Dropout (0.2) prevents overfitting
- Low learning rates (1e-5 to 1e-4) prevent catastrophic forgetting
- Mix real + XTTS data to maintain generalization

FILES GENERATED:
  models_xtts/
  ├── audio_projection.h5 (trainable model)
  ├── audio_projection_quantized.tflite (deployable)
  ├── query_embeddings.bin (pre-computed)
  └── training_plots/ (loss curves)

PRODUCTION WORKFLOW:
  Phase 1 (1 day): Quick validation with 50 samples → Expect 60-70%
  Phase 2 (1 week): Full training with 200+ samples → Expect 80-90%
  Phase 3 (Ongoing): Continuous improvement with user corrections

================================================================================
EXPERIMENT 3: WAKE WORD DETECTION TRAINING
Directory: wakeword_training_ipynb_poc/
Purpose: Train custom "Hey Daisy" wake word detector
================================================================================

FRAMEWORK: microWakeWord (GitHub: kahrendt/microWakeWord)
OBJECTIVE: Detect "Hey Daisy" while rejecting similar phrases

APPROACH:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Wake Word Detection Pipeline                                    │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                 │
│  1. Generate Positive Samples (Target phrases)                  │
│     ├─ Piper TTS: 1000 samples (100 per phonetic variation)    │
│     └─ TED speaker clips: 80 samples (10 per speaker)           │
│       Total positive: ~1080 samples                             │
│                                                                 │
│  2. Generate Negative Samples (Confusables to reject)           │
│     ├─ Partial phrases: "Hey", "Daisy" alone                   │
│     ├─ Similar-sounding: "Hey, lazy", "Hey, Davis"            │
│     ├─ XTTS generation: 50 samples per phrase                   │
│     └─ Total negative: ~500 samples                             │
│                                                                 │
│  3. Feature Extraction                                          │
│     └─ 40-bin log-mel spectrogram (30ms window, 10ms stride)    │
│                                                                 │
│  4. Model: MixNet (Depthwise-Separable CNN)                    │
│     └─ Streaming architecture (processes frame-by-frame)        │
│                                                                 │
│  5. Quantization                                               │
│     └─ Int8 TFLite (130 KB)                                    │
│                                                                 │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

TRAINING CONFIGURATION:
  Architecture: MixNet-based streaming model
  Input shape: 40-bin mel-spectrogram frames
  Training steps: 50000
  Learning rate: 0.0001 (fixed)
  Batch size: 100 (Colab) / 512 (Vast.ai)
  Negative class weight: 20× (heavily penalize false accepts)
  Loss metric: Sparse softmax cross-entropy
  Minimization metric: Loss

PHONETIC VARIATIONS TRAINED:
  ├─ "Hey Daisy" (base)
  ├─ "hey daisy" (lowercase)
  ├─ "hey day zee" (phonetic spelling)
  └─ ... (10+ variations to handle different pronunciations)

DATA GENERATION:
1. Piper TTS (LibriTTS-r medium model):
   - 10 phonetic variations × 100 samples = 1000 audio files
   - Diverse speaker characteristics
   - Fast synthesis (~1-2s per sample)

2. TED Speaker Sampling:
   - 8 real speakers from public TED datasets
   - 10 clips per speaker = 80 samples total
   - Natural speech with real accents/prosody

3. Confusable Negatives (prevents false accepts):
   - Partial phrases: "Hey" alone, "Daisy" alone
   - Similar-sounding: "Hey, lazy", "Hey, Davis", "Hey, daisy"
   - 50 samples per phrase via XTTS
   - Teaches model to reject partial matches

SAMPLE STATISTICS:
  ┌──────────────────────────┬──────────┐
  │ Category                 │ Samples  │
  ├──────────────────────────┼──────────┤
  │ Positive (Hey Daisy)     │ ~1080    │
  │ Negative (Confusables)   │  ~500    │
  │ Total                    │ ~1580    │
  └──────────────────────────┴──────────┘

DETECTION PARAMETERS (hey_daisy.json):
  {
    "probability_cutoff": 0.5,          # Minimum confidence
    "sliding_window_average_size": 10,   # Frames to average
    "min_high_frames": 6,                # Min high-confidence frames
    "min_frame_prob": 0.5,               # Frame-level threshold
    "cooldown_ms": 1500                  # Prevent rapid re-triggers
  }

OUTPUT MODEL:
  hey_daisy.tflite: 130 KB (quantized int8)
  hey_daisy.json: 262 bytes (configuration)

TUNING GUIDE:
  ┌────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Problem                │ Solution                             │
  ├────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Too many false accepts │ Increase probability_cutoff (0.6+)   │
  │ Too many misses        │ Decrease probability_cutoff (0.4-)   │
  │ Inconsistent detection │ Add more phonetic variations, retrain│
  │ Model too large        │ Reduce MixNet architecture size      │
  └────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────┘

DEPLOYMENT ON ESP32-S3:
  1. Copy hey_daisy.tflite to SD card: /models/hey_daisy.tflite
  2. Update sketch: #define MODEL_PATH "/models/hey_daisy.tflite"
  3. Configure thresholds if needed
  4. Test with real speech

PERFORMANCE METRICS:
  - False accept rate (FAR): Minimized via confusable negatives
  - False reject rate (FRR): Balanced via phonetic variations
  - Model size: 130 KB (fits in SRAM)
  - Inference latency: ~10ms per frame (streaming)

================================================================================
EXPERIMENT 4: YAMNET-1024 AUDIO EMBEDDING
Directory: yamnet_audio_embedding_ipynb_poc/
Purpose: Extract semantic audio embeddings for intent classification
================================================================================

APPROACH:
- Record 3-5 seconds of audio
- Generate mel-spectrogram via ESP-DSP FFT
- Run YAMNet-1024 inference (TensorFlow Lite)
- Extract 1024-D semantic embeddings

ARCHITECTURE:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ YAMNet-1024 Audio Embedding Pipeline (ESP32-S3)                │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                 │
│ 1. Audio Capture (Dual INMP441 microphones)                    │
│    ├─ Stereo I2S @ 16kHz, 32-bit samples                       │
│    ├─ 3-5 seconds recording                                    │
│    └─ Downmix to mono                                          │
│                                                                 │
│ 2. Feature Extraction (ESP-DSP accelerated)                    │
│    ├─ FFT size: 512 (25ms window @ 16kHz)                     │
│    ├─ Hop length: 160 samples (10ms stride)                   │
│    ├─ Mel filterbank: 64 bins                                  │
│    ├─ Frames: 96 (for 3 sec audio)                            │
│    ├─ Log mel-spectrogram: [1, 96, 64, 1] tensor              │
│    └─ Preprocessing time: ~500ms                               │
│                                                                 │
│ 3. YAMNet-1024 Inference (Dual-core optimized)                │
│    ├─ Core 0: Audio recording + preprocessing                  │
│    ├─ Core 1: TensorFlow Lite inference                        │
│    ├─ Architecture: MobileNetV1 (depthwise-separable)          │
│    ├─ Input: [1, 96, 64, 1]                                   │
│    ├─ Output: [1, 1024] embeddings                             │
│    └─ Inference time: 6-10 seconds (bottleneck)                │
│                                                                 │
│ 4. Output (JSON format)                                        │
│    └─ 1024-D float32 vector saved to SD card                   │
│                                                                 │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

MODEL OPTIONS:

1. YAMNet-1024 (Full)
   ├─ Model size: 3.9 MB (TFLite)
   ├─ Output dimension: 1024
   ├─ Inference: 6-10 seconds
   ├─ Best for: Rich semantic features
   └─ Deployment: PSRAM-based

2. YAMNet-256 (Lightweight)
   ├─ Model size: 167 KB (TFLite)
   ├─ Output dimension: 256
   ├─ Inference: 1-2 seconds (5× faster!)
   ├─ Best for: Speed-critical applications
   └─ Deployment: Fits in SRAM

MEL-SPECTROGRAM SPECIFICATION:
  FFT Window:     512 samples (25ms @ 16kHz)
  Hop length:     160 samples (10ms stride)
  Mel bins:       64
  Frequency range: 125-7500 Hz
  Window function: Hann
  Transformation: Log mel-filterbank energies

TIMING BREAKDOWN (3-sec audio, ESP32-S3 @ 240MHz):
  ┌────────────────────────┬──────────┬────────────┐
  │ Stage                  │ Duration │ % Total    │
  ├────────────────────────┼──────────┼────────────┤
  │ Audio recording        │ ~3000 ms │ 25%        │
  │ Mel-spectrogram        │  ~500 ms │  4%        │
  │ YAMNet inference       │ 6-10 sec │ 65% ⚠️ BN  │
  │ JSON write to SD       │  ~150 ms │  1%        │
  │ TOTAL                  │10-14 sec │ 100%       │
  └────────────────────────┴──────────┴────────────┘

MEMORY USAGE (PSRAM):
  ┌────────────────────────┬──────────┐
  │ Component              │ Size     │
  ├────────────────────────┼──────────┤
  │ Audio buffer (3s)      │ ~96 KB   │
  │ Mel-spectrogram        │ ~24 KB   │
  │ YAMNet-1024 weights    │ ~3.9 MB  │
  │ Tensor arena           │ ~400 KB  │
  │ Embeddings buffer      │ ~4 KB    │
  │ TOTAL                  │ ~4.4 MB  │
  │ Available PSRAM        │ 8 MB     │
  │ Headroom               │ ~3.6 MB  │
  └────────────────────────┴──────────┘

OUTPUT FORMAT (JSON):
  {
    "dimension": 1024,
    "embeddings": [
      0.234567,
      -0.123456,
      0.567890,
      ...
      (1024 values total)
    ]
  }

DEPLOYMENT STRATEGY:
  1. Download YAMNet-1024 from Kaggle (3.9 MB)
  2. Or: Use STM YAMNet-256 from HuggingFace (167 KB)
  3. Copy to SD card: /yamnet.tflite
  4. Upload sketch and run
  5. Extract embeddings for similarity search

PERFORMANCE NOTES:
  - YAMNet inference is the bottleneck (6-10 seconds)
  - Dual-core optimization helps but insufficient (TFLite ops are sequential)
  - Smaller YAMNet-256 recommended for real-time applications
  - Embeddings can be used for:
    - Audio similarity search (cosine distance)
    - Clustering (k-means on embeddings)
    - Classification (train simple classifier on top)
    - Voice identification (speaker recognition)

================================================================================
EXPERIMENT 5: LLM QA MEMORIZATION PoC
Directory: llm_qa_memorization_ipynb_poc/
Purpose: Proof-of-concept for tiny LLM on ESP32-S3
================================================================================

APPROACH:
- Train minimal LLM from scratch on Q&A pairs
- Achieve 80-90% accuracy on memorization
- Fit entire model + tokenizer in <1 MB
- Validate inference on ESP32-S3

ARCHITECTURE (Quick PoC Config):
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Tiny Transformer LLM (llama2.c port)                            │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                 │
│ Input: "<Q>question<A>" (tokenized)                            │
│        ↓                                                        │
│ Embedding Layer: vocab_size=227 → embedding_dim=128           │
│        ↓                                                        │
│ Transformer Stack (4 layers):                                  │
│   ├─ Self-attention: 128-D                                    │
│   ├─ Feed-forward: 128→512→128 (ReLU)                        │
│   ├─ Layer norm + Residuals                                   │
│   └─ × 4 layers                                               │
│        ↓                                                        │
│ Output projection: 128-D → vocab_size=227                     │
│        ↓                                                        │
│ Softmax: Probability distribution over vocabulary              │
│        ↓                                                        │
│ Sampling: Temperature + Top-P decoding                         │
│                                                                 │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

MODEL CONFIGURATION:
  Parameter                Value       Description
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Embedding dimension     128         Hidden size
  Number of layers        4           Transformer blocks
  Vocab size             227          Adaptive per dataset
  Max sequence length     256          Maximum context window
  Number of heads        8 (disabled) (Simplified for tiny config)
  Total parameters       ~500K        0.5M params

TOKENIZER SPECIFICATIONS:
  Type:                   SentencePiece BPE
  Vocab size:             227 (adaptive, min training corpus)
  Format:                 Binary (.bin) for llama2.c compat
  Special tokens:         <Q>, <A>, </A> (question/answer delimiters)
  Training source:        Q&A pairs from dataset

DATASET GENERATION:
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Phase 1: Create Q&A pairs from profile                           │
│ ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── │
│ Input: User profile (name, role, skills, dates, etc.)           │
│ Process:                                                          │
│   1. GPT-4 generates 50-100 Q&A variations                       │
│   2. Format: "<Q>question<A>answer</A>"                          │
│   3. Apply variation rules (5x repetition)                       │
│   4. Create train.txt and val.txt                                │
│                                                                  │
│ Example data:                                                    │
│   <Q>What is Alphons's email?<A>alphons@example.com</A>         │
│   <Q>Email of Alphons?<A>alphons@example.com</A>                │
│   <Q>What is his email address?<A>alphons@example.com</A>       │
│                                                                  │
│ Output: ~50-100 Q&A pairs with 5× variation = 250-500 total     │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

TRAINING PHASES:
Phase 1: Dataset Tokenization
  - Tokenize train/val split
  - Output: train.bin, val.bin (binary token streams)
  - Output: tokenizer.model, tokenizer.vocab (SentencePiece)
  - Output: tokenizer.bin (llama2.c format)

Phase 2: Model Training
  - Objective: Language modeling (next-token prediction)
  - Loss: Cross-entropy on vocabulary
  - Learning rate: 1e-4 (relatively high for small model)
  - Batch size: 32
  - Epochs: 50-100 (aggressive overfitting intended)
  - Duration: 10-20 minutes (Colab T4)

Phase 3: Quantization
  - Quantize float32 model to int8
  - Size reduction: 2 MB → 500 KB (4× compression)
  - Minimal accuracy loss (suitable for memorization)

TRAINING RESULTS:
  Architecture:     dim=128, layers=4, vocab=227
  Parameters:       ~500K
  Training time:    10-20 minutes (Colab)
  Final loss:       ~0.5-0.8 (on validation set)
  
  Quality metrics:
    - Exact match (input unchanged): 90%+
    - Similar phrasing: 80-90%
    - Paraphrased (heavy rephrase): 50-70%
    - Hallucination: Minimal (due to memorization)

MODEL SIZES:
  Float32:          ~2 MB
  Int8 quantized:   ~500 KB
  Tokenizer:        ~100-150 KB
  ────────────────────────────
  Total package:    <1 MB (leaves 7 MB for runtime!)

DEPLOYMENT STRATEGY:
1. Export model to llama2.c format (.bin)
2. Quantize to int8 for deployment
3. Upload both model and tokenizer to SD card
4. Load in llm_inference sketch for testing
5. Deploy to production firmware

INFERENCE METRICS (Estimated ESP32-S3):
  - Tokenization: ~1ms per token
  - Inference: ~25-30 tok/s (token generation speed)
  - Typical response: 5-10 tokens → ~200-400ms
  - Memory: Model + tokenizer = ~600-700 KB
  - Available heap/PSRAM: ~7.4 MB

EXPECTED QUALITY:
  Input variation (from training):   90%+ (exact memorization)
  Slight paraphrase:                 80-90%
  Moderate paraphrase:               70-80%
  Heavy paraphrase (novel phrasing): 50-70%

SCALING TO FULL PRODUCTION:

PoC Configuration:
  ├─ Model: 500K params
  ├─ Data: 50-100 Q&A pairs
  ├─ Training: 10-20 minutes
  └─ Accuracy: 80-90%

Production Configuration:
  ├─ Model: 3.5M params (dim=224, layers=6)
  ├─ Data: 1000-2000 Q&A pairs
  ├─ Training: Phase 1 (6-12 hours) + Phase 2 (1-2 hours)
  ├─ Model size: 3.5 MB (float32) → 900 KB (int8)
  ├─ + Tokenizer: ~150 KB
  └─ Total: ~1 MB (still fits!)

================================================================================
EXPERIMENT 6: LLM QA SCALED TRAINING
Directory: llm_qa_scaled_training/
Purpose: Full-scale personalized Q&A LLM training pipeline
================================================================================

APPROACH:
- Three-phase training: Stories pretraining → Profile fine-tuning → Q&A memorization
- Multiple model sizes (1M to 6M parameters)
- Multiple vocab sizes (512 to 1024 tokens)
- Produce optimized models for different hardware constraints

TRAINING PHASES:

Phase 1: TinyStories Pretraining (P1_stories)
  Objective:   Learn language fundamentals
  Data:        TinyStories dataset (~2M tokens)
  Steps:       10000 (with auto-scaling based on model size)
  Learning rate: 3e-4 (warm start)
  Goal:        Build general language understanding
  
Phase 2: Profile Fine-tuning (P2_profile)
  Objective:   Learn person-specific facts
  Data:        Mixed: 50% TinyStories + 50% profile context
  Steps:       5000 (scaled)
  Learning rate: 1e-4 (lower for fine-tuning)
  Goal:        Inject domain knowledge without forgetting language
  
Phase 3: Q&A Memorization (P3_qa)
  Objective:   Memorize exact Q&A pairs
  Data:        Profile-generated Q&A pairs
  Steps:       5000 (scaled)
  Learning rate: 5e-5 (very low for memorization)
  Goal:        Lock in exact responses with minimal drift

MODEL CONFIGURATIONS:

Configuration        Dim   Layers  Heads  Hidden  Vocab  Params
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1M (Minimal)        128    4       8      512    512    ~1M
2M (Small)          160    5       8      640    512    ~2M
3M (Medium)         176    6       8      704    768    ~3M
4M (Large)          192    6       8      768    1024   ~4M
5M (Larger)         208    7       8      832    1024   ~5M
6M (Full)           224    8       8      896    1024   ~6M

TOKENIZER OPTIONS:

Vocab Size   Compression  Quality   Use Case
────────────────────────────────────────────────
512          Best         Lower     Minimal footprint
768          Balanced     Good      Common choice
1024         Fine-grained Excellent  Production

MODEL SIZES (QUANTIZED INT8):

┌────────────┬──────────────┬───────────────┬──────────┐
│ Model      │ Float32      │ Int8 Quantized│ Token LR │
├────────────┼──────────────┼───────────────┼──────────┤
│ 1M-512TK   │ 4.1 MB       │ 1.1 MB        │ 3e-4     │
│ 3M-1024TK  │ 9.1 MB       │ 2.9 MB        │ 1e-4     │
│ 6M-1024TK  │ 22.0 MB      │ 6.0 MB        │ 5e-5     │
└────────────┴──────────────┴───────────────┴──────────┘

TRAINING DYNAMICS:

Phase 1 (Stories):        Phase 2 (Profile):      Phase 3 (Q&A):
Loss: 5.2 → 1.8          Loss: 1.8 → 0.9         Loss: 0.9 → 0.24
(Learn language)         (Learn person facts)    (Memorize Q&A)

LEARNING RATE SCHEDULE:
┌────────────────────────┬──────────┬──────────────────────┐
│ Phase                  │ LR       │ Reasoning            │
├────────────────────────┼──────────┼──────────────────────┤
│ P1_stories (pretraining)│ 3e-4    │ Warm start           │
│ P2_profile (fine-tune) │ 1e-4    │ 3.3× lower (prevent  │
│                        │         │ catastrophic forget) │
│ P3_qa (memorization)   │ 5e-5    │ 2× lower (lock in    │
│                        │         │ exact responses)     │
└────────────────────────┴──────────┴──────────────────────┘

TRAINING LOSSES OBSERVED (6M Model, 1024-vocab):

Phase 1 (Stories):
  Start: 5.22 (random init)
  Step 5000: 1.86 (rapid convergence)
  Step 10000: 1.82 (good language learning)

Phase 2 (Profile):
  Start: 1.82 (warm start from Phase 1)
  Step 5000: 0.90 (profile facts injected)

Phase 3 (Q&A):
  Start: 0.90 (warm start from Phase 2)
  Step 5000: 0.24 (excellent memorization!)
  Final: 0.2378 (best validation loss)

DEPLOYMENT:

Recommended Configuration for ESP32-S3:
  Model size: 6M (224-D)
  Vocab size: 1024
  Quantization: Int8
  Final size: ~6.0 MB (model) + 13 KB (tokenizer) ≈ 6.1 MB total
  
  This leaves ~2 MB for runtime buffers in 8 MB PSRAM

GENERATION PARAMETERS:
  Temperature: 0.7 (balanced random/deterministic)
  Top-P (nucleus): 0.9 (high diversity)
  Max tokens: 100 (typical response: 5-20 tokens)

INFERENCE PERFORMANCE (Estimated ESP32-S3):
  Token generation: 10-20 tok/sec (slower than PoC, more accurate)
  Typical query → response: 200-400 tokens → 10-40 seconds
  Memory: 6.1 MB model + ~1 MB runtime = ~7 MB PSRAM

FILE OUTPUTS:

Generated during training:
  output/
  ├── ajv009_6M_1024TK.bin (22 MB float32)
  ├── ajv009_6M_1024TK_q80.bin (6.0 MB int8) ← DEPLOY THIS
  ├── ajv009_1024TK.bin (tokenizer, 13 KB)
  ├── loss_history.csv (training metrics)
  └── training.log (full training output)

QUALITY EXPECTATIONS:

Exact match (training questions unchanged):    95%+
Similar phrasing (slight variation):           85-95%
Moderate paraphrase:                           75-85%
Heavy paraphrase (novel rephrase):             60-75%
Out-of-distribution (completely new):         30-40%

This is expected for memorization-based training!
